T–S · Question 1 — M3 Activation
Think of one person at your company — not your best friend, but someone you work with. Describe them in 3 sentences. Use: He/She is… / He/She has… / He/She is very… No names — just job, personality, appearance.
S–S · Question 2 — Possessive 's
Describe something that belongs to someone at your company. Use possessive 's: "[Name]'s desk is next to the window / [Name]'s manager is very strict / The manager's meeting is at 9."
Class · Question 3 — What's She/He Like?
Go around: each student answers "What's your manager like?" in 2 sentences. Use a personality adjective + a physical one. Partner guesses if it's a positive or negative description.
Teacher Note — M3 Error Preview
Watch for: "She is very organize" ✗ (adjective, not verb) → "She is very organized" ✅. "He have long hair" ✗ → "He has long hair" ✅. Write 3–4 on the board. Use in §5.
⚡ Quick Win — 20 seconds
Say out loud: "My manager is very organized and hardworking. She has short hair. Her office is next to mine." — to be + adjective + has + possessive 's. Four M3 structures. One breath.
5 min · 3 questions · Badge 👥 when done
§2
Speaking · The People at Vertex Logistics
3 rounds · Describe · Introduce · Compare people at work
8–10 min
T–S
New employee introduction. Ana García is introducing her new colleague Marcos to the Chicago team on a video call. Describe Marcos: his job, personality, and one physical detail. Use to be + adjective + has. Make it professional and positive.

"This is Marcos — he's our new logistics coordinator. He's very organized and reliable. He has a lot of experience with SAP. He's quite young but really hardworking — he's a great addition to the team!"

to be + job · adjectives: organized/reliable/hardworking · has + noun · quite/very modifiers

S–S
"What's your manager like?"
Partner A describes their real manager — personality + one physical detail + possessive ('s). Partner B listens and asks ONE follow-up Wh-question. Then switch. No negative descriptions — keep it professional!

"My manager's name is Roberto. He's very serious but also very fair. He has short dark hair and he's quite tall. His office is always clean and organized — just like him!"

possessive 's · adjectives (personality + physical) · very/quite modifiers · consistent tone

Class
Whose is this? Teacher puts 3 objects on a desk (a pen, a phone, a bag) and assigns them to fictional people with personalities. Students use possessive 's and adjectives to describe: "The pen is Ana's — she's very organized. The phone is David's — he's always busy."

"That's Ana's bag — it's very organized inside. The notebook is David's — he's always writing. Whose pen is this? It's the manager's — she's very strict about her things!"

possessive 's · Whose…? · adjective-noun link · personality in context

Teacher Note — GT Original: "actually ≠ actualmente"
Students often say "Actually she is very organized" meaning "Actualmente…" (currently). In English, "actually" means "en realidad / de hecho." Drill: "She's actually very patient" = "en realidad es muy paciente." One minute. High-return false friend for A1.1.

Teacher Note — very / quite modifiers
"Very" = intensifies. "Quite" = moderates (British) or intensifies (American). In Mexican corporate English with US clients: use "very" for strong, "quite" for moderate. Drill: "She's very strict" vs "She's quite strict" — which sounds stronger? Get opinions.
🗣️ Micro-Speaking — 45 seconds
Describe a real colleague using 3 words from the list. Add very or quite to at least one.
Model: "My colleague is very reliable and quite creative. She's also hardworking — she never misses a deadline."

§4
Colloquial · 4 Phrases for Talking About People
Introducing · describing personality · professional & natural
5 min
"This is [name] — he/she's our [job]."
The standard professional introduction in English. Clean, confident, and used at every level.
"This is Ana — she's our new project coordinator."
"What's he/she like?"
Asking about someone's personality — not appearance. Essential for team introductions and HR conversations.
"Is your new manager good?" — "What's she like?" "She's very patient."
"He/She's really good at [noun]."
Professional praise phrase. "Really good at" + noun (no gerund at A1.1). Common in performance reviews and recommendations.
"She's really good at presentations." Not: "…at presenting." ✗
"Just call me [first name]."
GT Original from M1 — now applied in M6 real context. North American/international corporate culture: first names always.
"Nice to meet you, Mr. Torres." — "Please, just call me David!"
Teacher Note — Chain Drill: Introductions
3-person chain: A introduces B to C. B introduces C to A. C introduces A to B. Each introduction must include: name + job + one personality adjective + "really good at [noun]." 90 seconds. Fast. Natural. This is the Exit Project in miniature.
§5
Grammar · Adjectives + Possessive 's — M3 in M6 Context
Problem → Tool · Adjective order · Possessive 's vs s' · Activities + Poll
10–12 min
🚨 Real Situation — New Team Introduction Email
Your Chicago manager asks you to write 3 lines about a colleague for the company newsletter:
"Ana es una coordinadora creativa y organizada. Tiene el pelo corto. La oficina de Ana está en el cuarto piso."
❓ How do you write this in correct English — adjective order, "has" for appearance, and possessive 's?
✅ Three Tools from M3
Tool 1 — Adjective order: Opinion → Size/Age → Physical → Nationality → Material + Noun
"a creative, organized coordinator" — opinion adjectives first, comma between them
Tool 2 — Appearance with HAS: "She has short hair / He has a beard" — NOT "She is short hair" ✗
Tool 3 — Possessive 's: "Ana's office" (one person) · "the managers' meeting" (plural)
Structure✅ Correct❌ Common error
Adjective + noun She's a creative coordinator.adjective BEFORE noun "She's a coordinator creative." ✗Spanish order — wrong in English
Appearance (has) He has short dark hair.have/has + adjective + noun "He is short hair." ✗Use HAS for physical features, not IS
Possessive 's (singular) Ana's desk / David's phonename + apostrophe + s "The desk of Ana" ✗Never use "of" for people's possessions
very / quite She's very organized. / quite friendly.modifier + adjective — no noun needed "She's very organize." ✗organized is an adjective, NOT a verb
⚠️ Top 3 M3 errors in M6 context — catch every time:
✘ "She is short hair" → ✅ She has short hair — physical features use HAS
✘ "He is a coordinator very organized" → ✅ He is a very organized coordinator — adjective before noun
✘ "The office of Ana" → ✅ Ana's office — possessive 's, never "of" for people

✏️ Activity A — Choose the Correct Form
1. David ___ short dark hair and a very friendly personality.
2. She's ___ new logistics coordinator at Vertex.
3. Which is CORRECT English word order?

🗣️ Micro-Speaking — 60 seconds
Describe a real colleague: name + job (with adjective before noun) + appearance (has) + one possessive 's sentence. Partner corrects any adjective order or "has" errors immediately.
✏️ Activity B — True or False? Description Rules
"She's very organize" — correct use of "organize" as an adjective after very.
"He has tall" — correct way to describe someone's height.
"David's laptop is on his desk" — correct use of possessive 's.
"She's a creative and organized coordinator" — adjective order is correct.
§6
Listening · Ana Describes Her New Team
Personality · appearance · possessive 's · adjectives in context · Badge 🎧
8–10 min
Ana Describes Her Team — Vertex Logistics, Celaya
A1.1 · M6 · S3A · Voice: ElevenLabs · Speed: 0.78
0:00 0:00

Hi! It's Ana García again — week three at Vertex Logistics! Today I want to tell you about the people on my team. They're really great.

First, there's my manager, Carmen López. She's very organized and quite strict — but in a good way. She always has a plan. Carmen's office is on the fourth floor, next to mine. She has long black hair and she's quite tall. She's very good at presentations. I think she's the most professional person I know.

Then there's David Torres — you know David, the operations manager. He's very friendly and always very busy. His desk is always full of papers, but he always knows where everything is! He has short hair and a beard. He's quite creative for an operations person — that's unusual! David's meetings are always interesting.

There's also a new analyst on the team — her name is Sofía Reyes. She's young — maybe 26 or 27. She has curly hair and she's very quiet in meetings, but she's really smart. Sofía's work is always excellent. She's really good at numbers — she's our data specialist.

And finally, there's Marcos — Marcos Ruiz. He's the logistics coordinator. He's tall and has short dark hair. He's very reliable and hardworking. Marcos's schedule is always full, but he's never late and never stressed. I want to be like Marcos!

So that's my team. Four amazing people. I'm very lucky. Actually — I mean, "en realidad" — I love this job!

📎 ElevenLabs: Voice — Ana (American English) · Speed 0.78 · A1.1 M6 S3A · ~195 words · adjectives + possessive 's + has throughout

Teacher Note — GT Original Alert in Script
At the end, Ana self-corrects: "Actually — I mean, 'en realidad'…" This is a deliberate teachable moment. Pause the audio here. Ask: "Why did Ana correct herself?" Students identify the false friend from M3. Reinforce: actually = en realidad, NOT actualmente.
1. How does Ana describe her manager Carmen?
2. What is Sofía Reyes really good at?
3. True or False: Marcos is often late and stressed at work.
4. True or False: Carmen's office is on the fourth floor, next to Ana's.

Teacher Note — Opinion Meter
After voting, pick students from each side. Force the grammar: "I agree because [adjective]…" / "I disagree because [adjective]…" — at least one sentence with a personality adjective AND one with an appearance description using HAS. Both structures in one justification.

Speaking Cards — Describe & Introduce
6 scenarios · 30 seconds · describe before you think
Card 1 / 6
CARD 1 OF 6
Describe your real manager to a new colleague — personality + appearance + possessive 's sentence. 4 sentences.
M3: He/She is very… / has… / [Name]'s office is… / really good at…
CARD 2 OF 6
Introduce yourself the way Ana would — job, personality, appearance, and what you're really good at.
M1+M3: "I'm a… / I'm very… / I have… / I'm really good at…"
CARD 3 OF 6
Describe Sofía Reyes from the listening — from memory. 3 sentences minimum. No notes.
M3 recall: young, quiet, smart, curly hair, data specialist — use what you remember
CARD 4 OF 6
Your team has a new person. Describe the ideal new colleague — what personality adjectives do you want? Why?
M3: "I want someone who is very… / quite… / really good at…"
CARD 5 OF 6
Describe 2 people in this room — WITHOUT saying their name. Class guesses who it is.
M3: personality + appearance + possessive + one routine (S2A: always/usually)
CARD 6 OF 6 ⭐
You are Ana. Describe your full team (Carmen, David, Sofía, Marcos) in 60 seconds — one sentence each. From memory.
All M3 tools: adjectives + has + 's + very/quite — integrate everything

✅ I Can Now… — Click each one when confident
I can describe a colleague's personality using: organized, reliable, patient, strict, creative, hardworking.
I know the rule: "She HAS short hair" — not "She IS short hair." HAS for physical features.
I can use possessive 's correctly: "Ana's office" / "David's phone" — never "the office of Ana."
I can put adjectives before the noun: "a very organized coordinator" — not "a coordinator organized."
I can introduce a colleague professionally: "This is [name] — she's our [job]. She's really good at [noun]."
"This is [name] — he's/she's our [job]."
Use this the next time you introduce a colleague to anyone — in English. One sentence, maximum professionalism.
"He/She's really good at [noun]."
Use in your next performance review, recommendation email, or team intro. Noun only — no gerund at A1.1.
"What's he/she like?"
Ask this about a new manager, a client, or a colleague before a meeting. It signals EQ and professionalism.
